source_text: Quibus duobus dominis neget posse seruiri, quia alterum offendi sit necesse alterum defendi, ipse declarat, deum proponens et mamonam. proinde mamonam quem intellegi uelit, si interpretem non habes, ab ipso potes discere. admonens enim nos de saecularibus suffragia nobis prospicere amicitiarum secundum serui illius exemplum, qui ab actu summotus dominicos debitores diminutis cautionibus releuat in subsidium sibi: et ego, inquit, dico uobis, facite uobis amicos de mamona iniustitiae, de nummo scilicet, de \' quo et seruus ille. iniustitiae enim auctorem et dominatorem totius saeculi nummum scimus omnes. cui famulatam uidens Pharisaeorum cupiditatem ammentauit hanc sententiam: non potestis deo seruire et mamonae. inridebant denique Pharisaei pecuniae cupidi, quod intellexissent scilicet mamonam de nummo dictum, ne quia existimet in mamona creatorem intellegendum et Christum a creatoris illos seruitute reuocasse.. quid nunc? potius ex hoc disce unum a Christo deum ostensum. duos enim dominos nominauit, deum et mamonam, crea. torem et nummum: denique non potestis deo seruire, utique ei, cui uidebantur seruire, et mamonam, cui magis destinabantur. quodsi ipse alium se ageret, non duos dominos, sed tres demonstrasset — et creator enim dominus, quia deus, et utique magis dominus quam mamonas magisque homini obseruandus, qua magis dominus —; quale est enim, ut qui mamonam dominum dixerat et cum domino iunxerat uero, ipsum dominum taceret, id est deum creatorem? aut numquid tacendo eo concessit seruiendum ei esse, si solummodo sibi et mamonae negauit posse seruiri? ita cum unum deum ponit, nominaturus et creatorem, si alius esset ipse, creatorem nominauit quem [dominum] sine alio [deo non] posuit. et illud itaque relucebit, quomodo dictum sit: (si) in mamona iniusto fideles non extitistis, quod uerum est quis uobis credet? in nummo scilicet iniusto, non in creatore, quem et Marcion iustum facit, et: si in alieno fideles inuenti non estis, meum quis dabit uobis? alienum enim debet esse a semis dei quod iniustum est. creator autem quomodo alienus erat Pharisaeis, proprius deus Iudaicae gentis? si ergo haec non cadunt in creatorem, sed in mamonam, \'quis uobis credet quod uerius est\'? et \'quis uobis dabit quod meum est\'? non potest quasi ali{en)us dixisse de alterius dei gratia. tunc enim uideretur ita dixisse, si eos in creatorem, non in mamonam infideles notando per creatoris mentionem distinctione se fecisset dei alterius, non commissuri suam ueritatem infidelibus creatoris, t quoniam tunc alterius uideri potest, si non ad hoc proponatur, ut a re, de qua agitur, separetur. Si autem et iustificantes se coram hominibus Pharisaei spem mercedis in homine ponebant, illo eos sensu increpabat, quo et propheta Hieremias: miser homo, qui spem habet in homine. si et adicit: scit autem deus corda uestra, illius dei uim commemorabat, (qui) lucernam se pronuntiarat scrutantem renes et corda. si superbiam tangit: quod elatum est apud homines perosum est deo, Esaiam ponit ante oculos: dies enim domini Sabaoth in omnem contumeliosum et superbum, in omnem sublimem et elatum, et humiliabuntur. Possum iam colligere, cur tanto aeuo deus Marcionis fuerit in occulto. expectabat, opinor, donec haec omnia disceret a creatore. didicit igitur usque ad Iohannis tempora atque ita exinde processit adnuntiare regnum dei dicens: lex et prophetae usque ad Iohannem; ex quo regnum dei adnuntiatur. quasi non et nos limitem quendam agnoscamus Iohannem constitutum inter uetera et noua, ad quem desineret Iudaismus et a quo inciperet Christianismus, non tamen, ut ab alia uirtute facta sit sedatio legis et prophetarum et initiatio euangelii, in quo est dei regnum.\' [Christus ipse.] nam id si probauimus, et uetera transitura et noua successura praedicari a creatore, si et Iohannes antecursor et praeparator ostenditur uiarum domini euangelium\', superducturi et regnum dei promulgaturi, et ex hoc iam, quod Iohannes uenit, ipse erit Christus qui Iohannem erit subsecutus ut antecursorem; et, si desierunt uetera et coeperunt ! noua interstite Iohanne, non erit mirum quod ex dispositione est creatoris, ut unde(unde) magis probetur ** quam ex legis et prophetarum in Iohannem occasu et exinde ortu regni dei. transeat igitur caelum et terra citius, sicut et lex et: prophetae, quam unus apexuerborum domini-nerbum enim, inquit Esaias, dei nostri manet in aeuum —: nam quoniam in Esaia iam tunc Christus, sermo scilicet et spiritus creatoris, Iohannem praedicarat — uocem clamantis in deserto: parate uiam domini — in hoc uenturum, ut legis et] prophetarum ordo exinde cessaret, per adimpletionem, non per destructionem, et regnum dei a Christo adnuntiaretur, I ideo subtexuit facilius elementa transitura quam uerba sua,\' confirmans hoc quoque, quod de Iohanne dixerat, non praeterisse.
pass_a_gloss: To whom He denies that it is possible to serve two lords, because it is necessary to offend one and defend the other, He Himself declares, setting forth God and mammon. Therefore, mammon, which He wishes to be understood, if you do not have an interpreter, you can learn from Him Himself. For, admonishing us to look out for worldly friendships according to the example of that servant, who, having been removed from office, relieves his lord's debtors by diminishing their securities for his own benefit: and I, He says, tell you, make friends for yourselves from mammon of unrighteousness, from money, of course, from which also that servant. For we know that money is the author and ruler of all the world's unrighteousness. Seeing the covetousness of the Pharisees, He strengthened this statement: you cannot serve God and mammon. Finally, the Pharisees, who were greedy for money, ridiculed, because they understood, of course, that mammon was spoken of in terms of money, not because they thought that the creator should be understood in mammon and that Christ had recalled them from the creator's servitude. What now? Rather, learn from this that Christ shows one God. For He named two lords, God and mammon, the creator and money: finally, you cannot serve God, certainly to Him, whom they seemed to serve, and mammon, to whom they were more devoted. But if He Himself were acting as another, He would have shown not two lords, but three — and the creator is indeed the Lord, because He is God, and certainly a greater Lord than mammon, and more to be observed by man, because He is a greater Lord —; what kind of thing is it, that He who said mammon was Lord and joined it with the Lord, should be silent about the Lord Himself, that is, the creator God? Or did He, by being silent about Him, concede that He should be served, if only He denied that it was possible to serve Him and mammon? Thus, when He sets forth one God, He names the creator, if He Himself were another, He named the creator, whom He set forth as Lord without another God. And that statement will also become clear, how it was said: if you have not been faithful in mammon of unrighteousness, who will trust you? Certainly, in unjust money, not in the creator, whom even Marcion makes just, and: if you have not been faithful in what is another's, who will give you what is mine? For what is another's should be alien to the semi-god, which is unjust. But how was the creator alien to the Pharisees, the proper God of the Jewish nation? If, therefore, these things do not fall upon the creator, but upon mammon, 'who will trust you, what is truer?' And 'who will give you what is mine?' He cannot have said this as if it were another's, by the grace of another god. For then He would seem to have said this, if He had noted them as unfaithful in the creator, not in mammon, by mentioning the creator, making a distinction, not committing His truth to the unfaithful creator, since then it could seem otherwise, if it were not proposed to separate Him from the thing about which He was speaking. But if the Pharisees, justifying themselves before men, were putting their hope of reward in men, He was rebuking them with the same sense in which the prophet Jeremiah said: woe to the man who puts his hope in man. And if He adds: but God knows your hearts, He was recalling the power of that God, who had declared Himself to be the searcher of kidneys and hearts. If He touches on pride: what is exalted among men is an abomination to God, He sets Isaiah before their eyes: for the day of the Lord of hosts shall be upon every arrogant and haughty one, and they shall be humbled. I can now gather why the God of Marcion was in hiding for so long. He was waiting, I think, until all these things were learned from the creator. Therefore, He learned up to the time of John and thus proceeded to announce the kingdom of God, saying: the law and the prophets were until John; from whom the kingdom of God is announced. As if we also do not recognize a certain boundary established by John between the old and the new, at which Judaism ceased and Christianity began, not, however, that the cessation of the law and the prophets and the initiation of the gospel, in which is the kingdom of God, was made by another virtue. For if we have proven this, that the old things are passing away and the new things are succeeding, as proclaimed by the creator, and John is shown to be the forerunner and preparer of the ways of the Lord, and the gospel is to be brought and the kingdom of God is to be proclaimed, and from this, now that John has come, Christ Himself will be the one who follows John as a forerunner; and if the old things have ceased and the new things have begun with John in between, it will not be surprising that this is from the disposition of the creator, so that it may be proven more than from the passing away of the law and the prophets in John and from the rising of the kingdom of God. Therefore, let heaven and earth pass away more quickly, just as the law and the prophets, than one dot of the Lord's words — for the word of our God remains forever —; for since in Isaiah, Christ, namely the speech and spirit of the creator, had already predicted John, saying: a voice crying in the desert: prepare the way of the Lord — in this, that the order of the law and the prophets would cease from then on, through fulfillment, not destruction, and the kingdom of God would be announced by Christ —, He subjoined that the elements would pass away more easily than His words, confirming also what He had said about John, that it had not passed away.

choices.why: The Latin word 'mamona' refers to wealth or riches, and in this context, it is used to describe the idea of serving God versus serving wealth.
The Latin word 'deus' refers to God, and in this context, it is used to describe the idea of serving God versus serving wealth.
The Latin word 'creator' refers to the creator God, and in this context, it is used to describe the idea of the creator God versus the God of Marcion.
The Latin word 'Iohannem' refers to John, and in this context, it is used to describe the idea of John as a forerunner and preparer of the ways of the Lord.
The Latin word 'euangelium' refers to the gospel, and in this context, it is used to describe the idea of the gospel being brought and the kingdom of God being proclaimed.

bible_refs.note: You cannot serve God and mammon
If you have not been faithful in the unrighteous mammon, who will trust you?

pass_b_english: He denies that anyone can serve two masters, because you inevitably offend one while defending the other, and He makes the point by pitting God against mammon. If you lack an interpreter for what He means by mammon, you can learn it straight from Him. He warns us to secure worldly friendships by following the example of the steward who, once fired, slashed his master's debtors' IOUs to buy himself a safety net. 'And I tell you,' He says, 'make friends for yourselves with the mammon of unrighteousness — that is, with money, the very stuff that steward handled' (Luke 16:13). Everyone knows money is the author and lord of all the world's injustice. When He saw the Pharisees' greed salivating over it, He drove the blade home: 'You cannot serve God and mammon.' The Pharisees, money-lovers to the bone, sneered — they knew perfectly well He meant money by mammon, not that the Creator was hiding inside the word and Christ had come to recall them from the Creator's service.

So learn this instead: Christ reveals one God. He names two masters — God and mammon, the Creator and money — and says you cannot serve God, the very One they claimed to serve, and mammon, the one they actually served. If He were peddling a different god, He would have had to present three lords, not two: the Creator is Lord because He is God, and He outranks mammon by an infinite margin, so He deserves far more allegiance. What kind of logic says the One who called mammon 'lord' and paired it with the true Lord then falls silent about the true Lord, the Creator God? Or did His silence concede that the Creator *should* be served, since He only denied you can serve *both*? By positing one God, He names the Creator; if He were someone else, He just named the Creator as Lord without any second deity. That clarifies the saying: 'If you have not been faithful in the mammon of unrighteousness, who will trust you with true riches?' (Luke 16:11). The referent is unjust money, not the Creator — whom Marcion even tries to paint as just — and: 'If you have not been faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is your own?' What belongs to another must be alien to the demiurge, since it is unjust. But how was the Creator alien to the Pharisees, the proper God of the Jewish nation? If these charges land on mammon, not the Creator, then 'who will trust you with what is truer?' and 'who will give you what is mine?' He cannot speak as if the true riches belonged to another god's grace. That would only make sense if He had charged them with unfaithfulness to the Creator rather than mammon, invoking the Creator to draw a distinction and withhold His truth from the Creator's unfaithful ones — since a second god only appears distinct if he is separated from the subject at hand.

If the Pharisees justified themselves before men and staked their reward on human approval, He rebuked them with the same thrust as Jeremiah: 'Cursed is the man who trusts in man.' When He adds, 'But God knows your hearts,' He invokes the power of that same God who declared Himself the searcher of kidneys and hearts. When He strikes at pride — 'What is exalted among men is an abomination to God' — He holds up Isaiah: 'The day of the Lord of hosts shall come upon every arrogant and haughty one, upon everyone lifted high, and they shall be humbled.' I can now see why Marcion's god stayed hidden for so long: he was waiting, I suppose, until he could learn all this from the Creator. So he took notes up to John's time, then launched his kingdom announcement: 'The Law and the Prophets were until John; from then on the kingdom of God is preached.' As if we don't also recognize John as the boundary marker between old and new, where Judaism ends and Christianity begins — not because a different power shut down the Law and Prophets and started the gospel where God's kingdom resides. If we have proven that the old passes and the new succeeds by the Creator's own proclamation, and John is shown as the forerunner and preparer of the Lord's ways, and the gospel is to be brought in and the kingdom proclaimed, then once John arrives, Christ must be the One who follows him as forerunner. And if the old ceased and the new began with John as the hinge, it should not surprise us that this follows the Creator's own design, so that it is proved even more decisively by the Law and Prophets' sunset in John and the kingdom's sunrise thereafter than by any other means. Therefore, heaven and earth will pass away sooner than one dot of the Lord's words — 'The word of our God stands forever' —; for in Isaiah, Christ, the Word and Spirit of the Creator, had already foretold John: 'A voice cries in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord' — signaling that the order of Law and Prophets would cease from that point through fulfillment, not destruction, and the kingdom of God would be announced by Christ. That is why He appended that the elements would pass away more easily than His words, confirming that what He said about John would not pass away either.
